newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. steps up pressure on IRA to declare ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. steps up pressure on IRA to declare ceasefire.

text.p: The United States has stepped up pressure on the Irish Republican Army (IRA) to declare a ceasefire, arguing that the election of British Prime Minister Tony Blair presents a new opportunity to address the conflict in Northern Ireland, senior U.S. officials said on Wednesday.

One official said that a top foreign policy adviser to U.S. President Bill Clinton had made the point in telephone calls to Gerry Adams, the leader of the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, and Martin McGuinness, Sinn Fein's chief negotiator.

"We said that Blair presented them a new opportunity (but that) that was an opportunity they had to seize," said one official, adding that "unconditional ceasefire was a condition for Sinn Fein participation in talks."

The thrust of the U.S. argument is that Blair's election on May 1, bringing the Labour party to power after 18 years of Tory rule in Britain, may give offer a chance to revive the Northern Ireland peace process.
The U.S. officials, who declined to be identified, were confirming a report in Wednesday's Financial Times.

A February 1996 bombing by the IRA in London shattered a 18-month ceasefire in the 28-year war aimed at ending British rule in Northern Ireland. Sectarian warfare has killed more than 3,200 people since 1969.

A more recent lull in hostilities, however, has improved the climate between the parties, with Britain last week resuming talks with Sinn Fein officials, although it still rules out ministerial-level meetings.
Political sources in Belfast said Sinn Fein would hold another round of talks with British officials on Wednesday to try to breathe new life into the peace process.

The talks, the second in a week since Britain relaxed its ban on contacts with Sinn Fein, come on the eve of a Dublin meeting between Britain's new Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam and Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring.
They also take place one day before Clinton visits London to hold his first official meeting with Blair and to attend a British Cabinet meeting, a rare honour for a foreign leader.

British and Sinn Fein officials said after their first meeting in 16 months last Wednesday that it was too soon to say whether prospects had improved for an early IRA ceasefire. But Sinn Fein said a start had been made on dealing with problems.

Northern Ireland has been tense for months after a resurgence in IRA guerrilla warfare and violence by pro-British Loyalist groups. Many people fear mid-year Protestant parades could spark serious street riots.
Britain and Ireland hope talks involving most Northern Ireland parties will rekindle the peace drive.
The talks, chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell, have been riven by inter-party wrangling. Adjourned in March, they are due to restart in Belfast on June 3.
One U.S. official said the atmosphere between the parties was clearly better, but said it was an open question whether sufficient progress had been made to lead to an IRA ceasefire.
